newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Seychelles struggles to attract oil companies.
newsitem.headline: Seychelles struggles to attract oil companies.

text.p: Better known as a tourist paradise, the Indian Ocean islands of the Seychelles are having a tough time trying to convince oil companies that it is a good prospecting bet.

"Our problem is that Seychelles is such a nice place that when technicians try to convince their management that prospectivity is good, they take it with a pinch of salt," Seychelles National Oil Company managing director Eddie Belle told Reuters on Friday at the Africa Upstream conference.

Asked why Seychelles wanted to get into the oil production business, he said that although tourism was the mainstay of the economy, income fluctuated depending on economic conditions in Europe, its main market.
"We would like to have other economic activities that will not make us rely too heavily on tourism," Belle said.
"That is one of the reasons we are also trying to promote our fishing and oil industry."
Belle admitted that the country's natural beauty was not the only factor working against its bid to become an oil producer.
Although geological surveys had shown that the Seychelles had oil sediments under a granite bedrock, no company had yet managed a successful oil strike.
The latest to try had been Britain's Enterprise Oil Plc, which pulled out in June after hitting a dry well at 3,500 metres last year.
Belle said he had evidence that if Enterprise had gone about 100 metres further, it would have hit the oil sediment.
"So right now we do not have anyone prospecting in Seychelles," he added.

In a bid to encourage oil companies, the government cut effective tax rates from 55 percent to 35 percent and royalty fees from 12.5 percent to five percent, with a further promise of dropping them altogether for marginal fields.
"Seychelles also has a very stable government and we therefore meet all the criteria that the majors have been talking about at this conference," Belle said.
He said he planned to launch an aggressive marketing drive, particularly targeting independent exploration companies because they appeared to be keener to take on challenges.
Asked whether an oil find would not pose environmental problems, Belle said oil production could be "clean" and would take place several miles out at sea from floating platforms.
There were no plans to build a refinery on the islands and all the crude would be exported for processing.
The Seychelles imports about 200,000 tonnes of refined products per year and generates all its electricity from oil, which Belle said bit hard into their foreign exchange earnings from tourism.
